items.title: Johnny DeDroit Interview, 1973-03-16
items.q: I knew him personally. He was my friend. ... And then I met him in New York, and we were palsy-weldy

ctx.x: Sure, but I want to ask you one question. Yes, we can. What about Mr. Grunwald? Did he play an instrument?

Mr. Grunwald was a very capable piano player, but he would only do it around us, because he was a big man. The Grunwald Music Store was named after Mr. Grunwald. I said to Louis a while ago, if I was a mistake, his name was Theodore, Theodore Grunwald. He was a fine musician and you couldn't fool him. He knew music, and he knew musicians when he heard of him. He was great on intonation, and that's what we had. When we played, we played in tune. That's what made our jazz just a little bit better than the other…

items.title: Johnny DeDroit Interview, 1969-12-04
items.q: I know he published Don't Mean a Thing If You Ain't Got That Swing, because I played the first three of them... So he brought Don't Mean a Thing and He Didn't Get That Swing.

ctx.x: I mean I'm like Louis Armstrong and I'm a contemporary. I helped him when he had patches in his pants. I helped many a colored man. I remember, I know he published Don't Mean a Thing If You Ain't Got That Swing, because I played the first three of them, Clarence Williams. And when I went to New York to play at Healy's Balkanades, and he called me up and he said, Johnny I've got some new tunes and they just fit you, and if you don't mind I'll come to rehearsal and tell you how I think they should be played. Not…
